title: Asset Classes
full_title: Equity, FX, Futures and Market-Neutral Books
tagline: How the same research sentence changes in ETFs, multi-asset books, FX, futures and long–short portfolios
summary: A rule that is well specified on one equity ETF is not yet a rule on a currency or a futures curve. This course specialises the earlier definitions: equity and ETF books, multi-asset trend and defensive mixes, spot FX quoting and lots, continuous futures and rolls, and market-neutral construction. Published losses are included on purpose.
overview: The open library is not a single market. Its long examples sit on equity ETFs, often sector funds, over one or two decades. A smaller set uses several asset classes at once, spot FX quoted in dollars, or a vendor’s continuous futures. Market-neutral examples go long and short, either as a pair or as a cross-sectional ranking. The mathematics of a moving average does not change across these pages. The instrument, the denominator of the return, the cost and the sample length do.

ETF chapters ask what an investor in the fund has already delegated: a basket, a rebalance, a fee. Studying an ETF trend rule is not the same as studying the constituents. Multi-asset chapters ask what 'defensive' means once bonds and gold, or whatever the specification lists, enter the universe. The course refuses to treat a ticker list as a recommendation.

FX and futures chapters are where casual ports of an equity rule fail. A dollar-quoted spot rate is a convention. A six-month momentum rule on several such rates, sized by inverse volatility, is the library’s time-series FX example, and the library reports a loss. A continuous futures series hides a roll that the real contract would have paid or received. Contract multipliers turn a weight into an integer. The course computes the integer.

Market-neutral chapters reconcile the weight constraints from Portfolio Construction with pairs and rankings from the signal courses. Dollar neutrality is not beta neutrality. A reported profit factor on a short futures sample is not a carry-home Sharpe ratio. Capacity — how much AUM the rule could have borne before its own trading moved the price — is stated as a question the library pages do not answer.
outcomes: Explain what an equity-ETF backtest does and does not say about the underlying constituents.
Specify a multi-asset trend or defensive book, including the universe and the fallback asset.
Compute a return on a dollar-quoted FX rate and size a position in lots.
Describe a continuous futures series, a roll, and the conversion from a weight to a whole number of contracts.
Build a dollar-neutral and a simple beta-neutral set of weights from a ranking or a pair.
Interpret a published loss on FX momentum, and a short futures sample, without flipping the sign into a recommendation.

history.title: A futures market for currencies
history.detail: Currency futures at the CME gave exchange-traded prices to what had been an interbank market, and fixed the contract as the unit of position.

history.title: Stock-index futures
history.detail: S&P 500 futures began trading at the CME on 21 April 1982, making a broad equity portfolio something a futures trend rule could hold long or short.

history.title: Exchange rates and the out-of-sample record
history.detail: Meese and Rogoff showed that standard macroeconomic models of the exchange rate did not beat a random walk out of sample. FX predictability has had to argue with that result ever since.

history.title: Equity baskets as a single price
history.detail: The listing of SPY made a capitalisation-weighted equity basket a traded instrument. An ETF backtest studies that instrument, including its fee and its creation mechanism only to the extent the price already reflects them.

history.title: A fully specified pairs book
history.detail: Gatev, Goetzmann and Rouwenhorst published a pairs rule whose matching, entry, exit and delay are explicit enough to argue with. Market-neutral chapters in this course use that standard of specification.
